availableCommands.name: $brooks-audit
availableCommands.description: Architecture audit that maps module dependencies, checks layering integrity, and flags structural decay across a codebase, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks to audit architecture, review folder/module structure, check for circular imports, understand how the codebase is organized, or asks "does this follow clean architecture?" or "why does everything depend on everything?". Also triggers for onboarding requests: "explain this codebase to a new developer" or "give me a codebase tour" (use onboarding mode). Do NOT trigger for: PR-level code review (use brooks-review) or line-level refactoring questions — this skill analyzes structural/module-level concerns, not individual functions.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-debt
availableCommands.description: Tech debt assessment that identifies, classifies, and prioritizes maintainability problems — helping teams build a refactoring roadmap — drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks about tech debt, refactoring priorities, what to clean up first, or asks "why is this so hard to change?", "what should we fix first?", or "how do I justify refactoring to management?". Do NOT trigger for: server health checks, HTTP /health endpoints, Kubernetes probes, database health, or application uptime — "health" in those contexts is infrastructure, not code quality. Also not for single-function refactoring questions.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-health
availableCommands.description: Combined codebase health dashboard that scores a project across all four quality dimensions — PR quality, architecture, tech debt, and test quality — in a single pass, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user wants an overall quality assessment, asks "how healthy is this codebase?", "run all the checks", "I need a health score before the release", or wants to onboard a new team with a quality overview. Do NOT trigger for: server health checks, HTTP health endpoints, Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes, database health, or application uptime. Also do not trigger when the user specifically requests only one dimension — use the corresponding focused skill instead (brooks-review / brooks-audit / brooks-debt / brooks-test).

availableCommands.name: $brooks-review

Triggers when: user asks to review code, check a PR, shares a diff or pastes code asking "does this look right?" / "any issues here?" / "ready to merge?", or asks for feedback on a function, class, or file. Also triggers when user mentions: code smells / refactoring / clean architecture / DDD / SOLID principles / Hyrum's Law / deep modules / tactical programming / conceptual integrity / Brooks's Law / Mythical Man-Month / second system effect. Do NOT trigger for: questions about how to write code from scratch, language syntax questions, or framework/tool questions where no existing code is shared.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-sweep
availableCommands.description: Full-sweep mode: runs a unified analysis across all quality dimensions — code decay, architecture, tech debt, and test quality — then applies fixes directly to the codebase. Safe changes are auto-applied; risky changes are confirmed before execution. Drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user wants to "fix everything", "sweep the codebase", "auto-fix all issues", "clean up the whole project", or asks for a single command that both diagnoses and remediates quality problems. Do NOT trigger for: read-only audits or health reports where the user only wants findings without code changes; single-dimension reviews (use the focused skill instead: brooks-review / brooks-audit / brooks-debt / brooks-test); server health checks, HTTP /health endpoints, Kubernetes probes, database health, or application uptime.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-test

Triggers when: user asks about test quality, shares test files for review, or expresses frustration: "tests keep breaking whenever I change anything", "our tests take forever", "tests pass but bugs still reach production", or "we have too many mocks". - `must_fix`, `missing_evidence`, `open_risks`, and `failure.reason` mean unresolved blockers for the current decision.

# Codex Intake Product Review

Workstream: ws-20261011T044656Z-BMDJ
Node: intake.codex_product_review
Template: intake-codex-product-review
Ledger: .agent/workstreams/ws-20261011T044656Z-BMDJ

Ledger write policy:

- Do not create, edit, or delete files under .agent/.
- Only the orchestrator writes run ledger artifacts.
- Return your artifact in stdout using the contract below.

You are Codex acting as an external reviewer. Review the intake artifact from product manager, architect, and final-user perspectives.

Do not modify files. Do not perform line-by-line code review. Focus on product completeness, architectural fit, missing assumptions, and whether the workflow can safely move forward.

Treat the typed `task_contract_proposal` result in the intake context as the candidate shared task contract. Review it by principles, not by formatting nitpicks.

The current node's `AgentResultEnvelope`, JSON-only output, and workflow-routing protocol are enforced independently by the orchestrator's Output Contract. Do not require the task proposal to duplicate those harness protocols, and do not return `NEEDS_REVISION` solely because they are absent from proposal fields.

## Contract Review Principles

# Contract Review Principles

- Intent fidelity: the proposal must preserve the user's original intent.
- Explicit-requirement coverage: every user-stated objective, scope boundary, behavior constraint, acceptance criterion, and verification requirement must appear in a binding proposal field; `risk_areas`, `open_questions`, and `evidence_refs` do not preserve requirements.
- Protocol ownership: harness output and routing protocols belong to the orchestrator's node Output Contract and must not be duplicated into the product task proposal.
- Semantic neutrality: the proposal must not broaden or narrow accepted input, output, scope, or observable behavior based on an unstated implementation preference or language-specific edge case.
- Typed scope authority: intake file entries are proposals, not authorization. GOAL approval fixes the objective, acceptance and exclusions, not an implementation file set. Design and plan review produce the candidate for later exact EXECUTION approval. Only the approved EXECUTION `scope.included` is the exhaustive authorization set for permitted repository changes; each entry names one exact repository-relative path and `CREATE` or `MODIFY`. It does not require every declared path to be changed. Acceptance criteria, constraints, risks, and other prose cannot authorize an undeclared path. Never request an illustrative or non-exhaustive EXECUTION scope. A scope gap must request concrete typed path-and-operation changes.
- Non-goal clarity: boundaries must prevent unrelated refactors and scope creep.
- Verifiability: acceptance criteria must be observable by self-test, reviewer inspection, or user acceptance.
- Evidence grounding: important claims should point to user request, repo files, or prior artifacts.
- Risk coverage: risk areas should expose product, architecture, user, and data-safety risks relevant to the task.
- Human boundary: ask for human input only for real product/risk decisions, not JSON formatting or process validation.

If the proposal is missing, polluted by ledger metadata, materially inconsistent with the user request, or too vague to guide implementation, return `NEEDS_REVISION`. If the task has real product ambiguity that an agent should not decide, return `NEEDS_REVISION` or `BLOCKED` with the specific question for the next gate.

# 换行规范化函数

在新的本地 Python 仓库提供 `normalize_newlines(text: str) -> str`：将 CRLF 和单独 CR 转为 LF，保留其他字符、空串、已有 LF，以及末尾有无换行。只使用 Python 标准库，不引入第三方依赖、网络、数据库、浏览器、后台服务或机器配置修改。

提供 unittest 测试和 README 用法。建议文件为 `src/normalize_text.py`、`tests/test_normalize_text.py`、`README.md`；它们是待设计与计划确认的提案，最终具体文件和 CREATE/MODIFY 在实现前单独批准。

验收：

- AC-1：空串、纯 LF、CRLF、单 CR、混合换行、Unicode、末尾有/无换行、连续空行至少八种输入有明确期望，重复规范化保持相同结果。
- AC-2：实际执行测试，实际输出明确显示覆盖数、零 failure/error，并与测试源码中的案例相符。本任务不要求工具提供独立测量的真实退出码，但测试完成状态或文字结论本身不能替代实际输入/输出与测试结果。
- AC-3：README 例子与代码一致，包含导入和典型混合换行输入/输出；实际读取源码/文档或执行例子支持这一结论。

Use when Codex is asked to understand a project, make cross-module changes, review architecture, diagnose UI/CLI/API/ledger state disagreement, modify workflow/orchestrator/state-machine/agent-lifecycle code, prepare open-source architecture docs, or when the risk is that a local fix will bypass domain boundaries.

availableCommands.name: $architecture-governance-review
availableCommands.description: Use when reviewing or designing architecture, workflow/orchestrator changes, automation, backend service boundaries, agent lifecycle systems, recovery/compensation, human gates, delivery flows, or when code appears to drift from domain boundaries. Use before implementation or during review when the risk is overengineering, scattered if/else rules, unclear ownership, hidden state, cost/token runaway, or UI/CLI/API/ledger disagreement.

availableCommands.name: $article-review-zh
availableCommands.description: Use when reviewing Chinese articles, WeChat drafts, technical essays, whitepaper-to-article rewrites, or series posts for editorial readiness, structure, professional credibility, reach, author voice, or AI-writing risk before rewriting.

availableCommands.name: $boundary-first-engineering
availableCommands.description: Use before changing or reviewing systems with non-trivial state, lifecycle transitions, workflow/orchestration, external adapters, retries, recovery, compensation, async workers, queues, schedulers, human decisions, structured contracts, events, ledgers, projections, dashboards, reports, UI/CLI/API status, or completion semantics. Trigger when symptoms include repeated local fixes, ambiguous completion, stale running state, duplicated status logic, natural-language parsing drift, hidden evidence, projection disagreement, retry/resume confusion, terminal-state leaks, or any temptation to fix a state bug with handler-local if/else.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-audit
availableCommands.description: Architecture audit that maps module dependencies, checks layering integrity, and flags structural decay across a codebase, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks to audit architecture, review folder/module structure, check for circular imports, understand how the codebase is organized, or asks "does this follow clean architecture?" or "why does everything depend on everything?". Also triggers for onboarding requests: "explain this codebase to a new developer" or "give me a codebase tour" (use onboarding mode). Do NOT trigger for: PR-level code review (use brooks-review) or line-level refactoring questions — this skill analyzes structural/module-level concerns, not individual functions.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-debt
availableCommands.description: Tech debt assessment that identifies, classifies, and prioritizes maintainability problems — helping teams build a refactoring roadmap — drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks about tech debt, refactoring priorities, what to clean up first, or asks "why is this so hard to change?", "what should we fix first?", or "how do I justify refactoring to management?". Do NOT trigger for: server health checks, HTTP /health endpoints, Kubernetes probes, database health, or application uptime — "health" in those contexts is infrastructure, not code quality. Also not for single-function refactoring questions.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-health
availableCommands.description: Combined codebase health dashboard that scores a project across all four quality dimensions — PR quality, architecture, tech debt, and test quality — in a single pass, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user wants an overall quality assessment, asks "how healthy is this codebase?", "run all the checks", "I need a health score before the release", or wants to onboard a new team with a quality overview. Do NOT trigger for: server health checks, HTTP health endpoints, Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes, database health, or application uptime. Also do not trigger when the user specifically requests only one dimension — use the corresponding focused skill instead (brooks-review / brooks-audit / brooks-debt / brooks-test).

availableCommands.name: $brooks-review
availableCommands.description: PR code review that surfaces decay risks, design smells, and maintainability issues with concrete Symptom → Source → Consequence → Remedy findings, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks to review code, check a PR, shares a diff or pastes code asking "does this look right?" / "any issues here?" / "ready to merge?", or asks for feedback on a function, class, or file. Also triggers when user mentions: code smells / refactoring / clean architecture / DDD / SOLID principles / Hyrum's Law / deep modules / tactical programming / conceptual integrity / Brooks's Law / Mythical Man-Month / second system effect. Do NOT trigger for: questions about how to write code from scratch, language syntax questions, or framework/tool questions where no existing code is shared.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-sweep
availableCommands.description: Full-sweep mode: runs a unified analysis across all quality dimensions — code decay, architecture, tech debt, and test quality — then applies fixes directly to the codebase. Safe changes are auto-applied; risky changes are confirmed before execution. Drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user wants to "fix everything", "sweep the codebase", "auto-fix all issues", "clean up the whole project", or asks for a single command that both diagnoses and remediates quality problems. Do NOT trigger for: read-only audits or health reports where the user only wants findings without code changes; single-dimension reviews (use the focused skill instead: brooks-review / brooks-audit / brooks-debt / brooks-test); server health checks, HTTP /health endpoints, Kubernetes probes, database health, or application uptime.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-test
availableCommands.description: Test quality review drawing on twelve classic engineering books — with primary focus on xUnit Test Patterns, The Art of Unit Testing, How Google Tests Software, and Working Effectively with Legacy Code — that diagnoses structural problems in an existing test suite: brittleness, mock abuse, coverage illusions, slow execution, poor readability. Triggers when: user asks about test quality, shares test files for review, or expresses frustration: "tests keep breaking whenever I change anything", "our tests take forever", "tests pass but bugs still reach production", or "we have too many mocks". Do NOT trigger for: writing new tests from scratch (use the regular test-writing workflow) or testing framework/syntax questions — this skill reviews an existing suite for structural quality problems, not individual test authoring.

availableCommands.name: $eli5

Also trigger when the user mentions wanting to understand something at a particular level, or asks for an explanation targeting a non-technical audience. Even partial matches like 'explain to my wife' or 'tell my boss' should trigger this skill.

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-cli

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-debugging
availableCommands.description: Use when the user is debugging a bug, tracing an error, or asking why something fails. Examples: "Why is X failing?", "Where does this error come from?", "Trace this bug"

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-exploring
availableCommands.description: Use when the user asks how code works, wants to understand architecture, trace execution flows, or explore unfamiliar parts of the codebase. Examples: "How does X work?", "What calls this function?", "Show me the auth flow"

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-guide
availableCommands.description: Use when the user asks about GitNexus itself — available tools, how to query the knowledge graph, MCP resources, graph schema, or workflow reference. Examples: "What GitNexus tools are available?", "How do I use GitNexus?"

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-impact-analysis
availableCommands.description: Use when the user wants to know what will break if they change something, or needs safety analysis before editing code. Examples: "Is it safe to change X?", "What depends on this?", "What will break?"

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-lfg
availableCommands.description: Use when the user wants the GitNexus engineering pipeline run end-to-end on a task: gitnexus-plan (plan depth chosen up front), a blocking gate to execute with gitnexus-work or stop, finishing with a gitnexus-review of the result. Examples: "/gitnexus-lfg Add retry support to the ingestion pipeline", "run the gitnexus pipeline on this", "plan, build and review this feature".

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-pdg-query
availableCommands.description: Use when querying or extending GitNexus's PDG control/data-dependence surface (the `pdg_query` MCP tool, CDG/REACHING_DEF edges), or reasoning about "what controls X" / "where does Y flow" / guard clauses. Examples: "what guards this statement?", "trace this variable within the function", "why is the pdg_query result empty?", "add a CDG query".

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-plan

Also strengthens existing plans via Deepen mode. Examples: "/gitnexus-plan Add retry support to the ingestion pipeline", "/gitnexus-plan deepen docs/plans/<plan>.md", "plan this change using the knowledge graph".

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-refactoring
availableCommands.description: Use when the user wants to rename, extract, split, move, or restructure code safely. Examples: "Rename this function", "Extract this into a module", "Refactor this class", "Move this to a separate file"

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-review
availableCommands.description: Review code changes with GitNexus from a GitHub PR URL or number, a branch/ref or commit range, or local staged, unstaged, and untracked changes. Use when the user asks for a code review, merge-risk assessment, regression hunt, missing-test analysis, or a verdict on whether a PR, branch, commit range, or local diff is safe.

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-taint-analysis
availableCommands.description: Use when working on, reviewing, or extending GitNexus's CFG/taint/PDG subsystem (the `--pdg` layers), or when reasoning about source→sink data-flow findings. Examples: "How does taint analysis work here?", "Why didn't explain find this flow?", "Add a new sink/source", "Review the interprocedural taint code".

availableCommands.name: $gitnexus:gitnexus-work
availableCommands.description: Use when executing an engineering plan produced by gitnexus-plan (or a small bounded task directly) — implements step by step with GitNexus impact checks before every symbol edit, tests from the plan's scenarios, and detect_changes gating every commit. Examples: "/gitnexus-work docs/plans/2026-07-11-gitnexus-plan-ingestion-retry.md", "/gitnexus-work" (latest plan), "execute the plan".

availableCommands.name: $ponytail

availableCommands.name: $architecture-cartographer
availableCommands.description: Map a complex or unfamiliar codebase before changing it. Use when Codex is asked to understand a project, make cross-module changes, review architecture, diagnose UI/CLI/API/ledger state disagreement, modify workflow/orchestrator/state-machine/agent-lifecycle code, prepare open-source architecture docs, or when the risk is that a local fix will bypass domain boundaries.

availableCommands.name: $architecture-governance-review
availableCommands.description: Use when reviewing or designing architecture, workflow/orchestrator changes, automation, backend service boundaries, agent lifecycle systems, recovery/compensation, human gates, delivery flows, or when code appears to drift from domain boundaries. Use before implementation or during review when the risk is overengineering, scattered if/else rules, unclear ownership, hidden state, cost/token runaway, or UI/CLI/API/ledger disagreement.

availableCommands.name: $article-review-zh
availableCommands.description: Use when reviewing Chinese articles, WeChat drafts, technical essays, whitepaper-to-article rewrites, or series posts for editorial readiness, structure, professional credibility, reach, author voice, or AI-writing risk before rewriting.

availableCommands.name: $boundary-first-engineering
availableCommands.description: Use before changing or reviewing systems with non-trivial state, lifecycle transitions, workflow/orchestration, external adapters, retries, recovery, compensation, async workers, queues, schedulers, human decisions, structured contracts, events, ledgers, projections, dashboards, reports, UI/CLI/API status, or completion semantics. Trigger when symptoms include repeated local fixes, ambiguous completion, stale running state, duplicated status logic, natural-language parsing drift, hidden evidence, projection disagreement, retry/resume confusion, terminal-state leaks, or any temptation to fix a state bug with handler-local if/else.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-audit
availableCommands.description: Architecture audit that maps module dependencies, checks layering integrity, and flags structural decay across a codebase, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks to audit architecture, review folder/module structure, check for circular imports, understand how the codebase is organized, or asks "does this follow clean architecture?" or "why does everything depend on everything?". Also triggers for onboarding requests: "explain this codebase to a new developer" or "give me a codebase tour" (use onboarding mode). Do NOT trigger for: PR-level code review (use brooks-review) or line-level refactoring questions — this skill analyzes structural/module-level concerns, not individual functions.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-debt
availableCommands.description: Tech debt assessment that identifies, classifies, and prioritizes maintainability problems — helping teams build a refactoring roadmap — drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks about tech debt, refactoring priorities, what to clean up first, or asks "why is this so hard to change?", "what should we fix first?", or "how do I justify refactoring to management?". Do NOT trigger for: server health checks, HTTP /health endpoints, Kubernetes probes, database health, or application uptime — "health" in those contexts is infrastructure, not code quality. Also not for single-function refactoring questions.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-health
availableCommands.description: Combined codebase health dashboard that scores a project across all four quality dimensions — PR quality, architecture, tech debt, and test quality — in a single pass, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user wants an overall quality assessment, asks "how healthy is this codebase?", "run all the checks", "I need a health score before the release", or wants to onboard a new team with a quality overview. Do NOT trigger for: server health checks, HTTP health endpoints, Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes, database health, or application uptime. Also do not trigger when the user specifically requests only one dimension — use the corresponding focused skill instead (brooks-review / brooks-audit / brooks-debt / brooks-test).

availableCommands.name: $brooks-review
availableCommands.description: PR code review that surfaces decay risks, design smells, and maintainability issues with concrete Symptom → Source → Consequence → Remedy findings, drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user asks to review code, check a PR, shares a diff or pastes code asking "does this look right?" / "any issues here?" / "ready to merge?", or asks for feedback on a function, class, or file. Also triggers when user mentions: code smells / refactoring / clean architecture / DDD / SOLID principles / Hyrum's Law / deep modules / tactical programming / conceptual integrity / Brooks's Law / Mythical Man-Month / second system effect. Do NOT trigger for: questions about how to write code from scratch, language syntax questions, or framework/tool questions where no existing code is shared.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-sweep
availableCommands.description: Full-sweep mode: runs a unified analysis across all quality dimensions — code decay, architecture, tech debt, and test quality — then applies fixes directly to the codebase. Safe changes are auto-applied; risky changes are confirmed before execution. Drawing on twelve classic engineering books. Triggers when: user wants to "fix everything", "sweep the codebase", "auto-fix all issues", "clean up the whole project", or asks for a single command that both diagnoses and remediates quality problems. Do NOT trigger for: read-only audits or health reports where the user only wants findings without code changes; single-dimension reviews (use the focused skill instead: brooks-review / brooks-audit / brooks-debt / brooks-test); server health checks, HTTP /health endpoints, Kubernetes probes, database health, or application uptime.

availableCommands.name: $brooks-test
availableCommands.description: Test quality review drawing on twelve classic engineering books — with primary focus on xUnit Test Patterns, The Art of Unit Testing, How Google Tests Software, and Working Effectively with Legacy Code — that diagnoses structural problems in an existing test suite: brittleness, mock abuse, coverage illusions, slow execution, poor readability. Triggers when: user asks about test quality, shares test files for review, or expresses frustration: "tests keep breaking whenever I change anything", "our tests take forever", "tests pass but bugs still reach production", or "we have too many mocks". Do NOT trigger for: writing new tests from scratch (use the regular test-writing workflow) or testing framework/syntax questions — this skill reviews an existing suite for structural quality problems, not individual test authoring.

You are Codex acting as an external reviewer. Review the intake artifact from product manager, architect, and final-user perspectives.

Do not modify files. Do not perform line-by-line code review. Focus on product completeness, architectural fit, missing assumptions, and whether the workflow can safely move forward.

Treat the typed `task_contract_proposal` result in the intake context as the candidate shared task contract. Review it by principles, not by formatting nitpicks.

The current node's `AgentResultEnvelope`, JSON-only output, and workflow-routing protocol are enforced independently by the orchestrator's Output Contract. Do not require the task proposal to duplicate those harness protocols, and do not return `NEEDS_REVISION` solely because they are absent from proposal fields.

## Contract Review Principles

# Contract Review Principles

- Intent fidelity: the proposal must preserve the user's original intent.
- Explicit-requirement coverage: every user-stated objective, scope boundary, behavior constraint, acceptance criterion, and verification requirement must appear in a binding proposal field; `risk_areas`, `open_questions`, and `evidence_refs` do not preserve requirements.
- Protocol ownership: harness output and routing protocols belong to the orchestrator's node Output Contract and must not be duplicated into the product task proposal.
- Semantic neutrality: the proposal must not broaden or narrow accepted input, output, scope, or observable behavior based on an unstated implementation preference or language-specific edge case.
- Typed scope authority: intake file entries are proposals, not authorization. GOAL approval fixes the objective, acceptance and exclusions, not an implementation file set. Design and plan review produce the candidate for later exact EXECUTION approval. Only the approved EXECUTION `scope.included` is the exhaustive authorization set for permitted repository changes; each entry names one exact repository-relative path and `CREATE` or `MODIFY`. It does not require every declared path to be changed. Acceptance criteria, constraints, risks, and other prose cannot authorize an undeclared path. Never request an illustrative or non-exhaustive EXECUTION scope. A scope gap must request concrete typed path-and-operation changes.
- Non-goal clarity: boundaries must prevent unrelated refactors and scope creep.
- Verifiability: acceptance criteria must be observable by self-test, reviewer inspection, or user acceptance.
- Evidence grounding: important claims should point to user request, repo files, or prior artifacts.
- Risk coverage: risk areas should expose product, architecture, user, and data-safety risks relevant to the task.
- Human boundary: ask for human input only for real product/risk decisions, not JSON formatting or process validation.

If the proposal is missing, polluted by ledger metadata, materially inconsistent with the user request, or too vague to guide implementation, return `NEEDS_REVISION`. If the task has real product ambiguity that an agent should not decide, return `NEEDS_REVISION` or `BLOCKED` with the specific question for the next gate.

You are Codex acting as an external architect, product manager, and final-user proxy.

Complete-current-design review discipline:
